findings.diagnosis: The prompt lets cuts split a phrase from a following dependent clause or clausal complement (subordinating/relative/‘that’–type clauses), underestimating how much meaning and entailment are lost when the clause is separated.
findings.evidence: en_us_577, en_us_1527, en_us_1144, en_us_381, en_us_633, en_us_872, en_us_101, en_us_549, en_us_738, en_us_1570, en_us_1601, en_us_368, en_us_309, en_us_276, en_us_543 — each policy cut occurs immediately before a dependent (subordinating or relative) clause or clausal complement that the target keeps attached; those policy cuts raise contradiction or destroy cohesion.
findings.type_predicate: Markers that immediately precede a dependent clause (a subordinating clause, relative clause, or clausal complement that completes/restricts the preceding phrase).

edit.text: Do not cut where the next constituent is a dependent clause (subordinating clause, relative clause, or clausal complement) that completes, restricts, or names the preceding phrase; keep that clause attached to its head.

findings.diagnosis: When multiple candidate cuts are all bad for the same attachment, the prompt fails to prefer the safer (later) cut that preserves a head with its clausal complement, causing misordered choices among similarly judged positions.
findings.evidence: en_us_633, en_us_381, en_us_30, en_us_481, en_us_1116 — each sentence contains a pair of candidate cuts where one cut would split a head from its clausal complement and the other would preserve them; the measurement prefers preserving the head+complement but the prompt ranks the splitter higher.
findings.type_predicate: Sentences that contain two candidate cuts around the same clause: one immediately before a dependent/clausal complement and another immediately after that complement (both markers present).

edit.text: Order rule: when choosing between two cuts that either split or preserve a head plus its clausal complement, prefer the cut that preserves the head and its complement (i.e., the later cut).
